sections.summary: The Sanhedrin hands Jesus over to Pilate; Pilate asks if he is the King of the Jews; Jesus answers ambiguously ('You say so') and then falls silent before the accusations, fulfilling the Suffering Servant's silence of Isaiah 53:7.

The crowd, stirred by the chief priests, chooses the release of Barabbas (an insurrectionist whose name means 'son of the father') over Jesus; Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd rather than render justice, has Jesus flogged and hands him over for crucifixion.

sections.section_title: The Soldiers' Mockery -- An Ironic Enthronement
sections.summary: Roman soldiers perform a mock coronation with purple cloak, crown of thorns, and the salute 'Hail, King of the Jews,' parodying imperial ceremony in a scene the author presents as ironically true -- every mocking gesture unwittingly enacts the real enthronement of Jesus.

Simon of Cyrene, a bystander identified as the father of Alexander and Rufus, is compelled by soldiers to carry Jesus's cross -- literally doing what the disciples were called to do figuratively (8:34) while the disciples themselves are absent.

Jesus is crucified at Golgotha at the third hour, refuses wine mixed with myrrh, and the soldiers divide his garments by casting lots (fulfilling Psalm 22:18); the inscription of the charge reads 'The King of the Jews,' functioning as both criminal charge and christological proclamation.

Jesus is crucified between two rebels (occupying the 'right and left' positions James and John requested), mocked by passersby who shake their heads (Psalm 22:7), and taunted by the chief priests who declare 'He saved others; He cannot save himself' -- a statement the author presents as profoundly true in ways the mockers do not intend, since the ransom logic of 10:45 requires that saving others and saving himself are mutually exclusive.

sections.section_title: Darkness, Death, the Veil, and the Centurion
sections.summary: Darkness covers the land from the sixth to the ninth hour; Jesus cries Psalm 22:1 ('My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?'), invoking a psalm that moves from abandonment through deliverance to universal worship; at his death the temple veil tears from top to bottom (divine action removing the barrier between God and humanity, using the same verb as the heavens 'tearing' at baptism in 1:10); and a Roman centurion declares 'Truly this Man was God's Son,' completing the christological arc from the narrator's opening (1:1) through the divine voice (1:11, 9:7) to this Gentile confession at the cross.

Women who followed and served Jesus in Galilee -- Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, Salome, and many others -- are identified as watching from a distance, having remained present through the crucifixion while the male disciples fled.

Joseph of Arimathea, a respected council member waiting for the kingdom of God, boldly asks Pilate for the body; the centurion confirms death; Joseph wraps the body in linen and places it in a rock-hewn tomb sealed with a stone; Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses observe the burial location, maintaining the chain of witness.
